Putting greens for Narcoossee's golfers and big side yards

A backyard putting green in Narcoossee runs $14–$30 per square foot as of September 2026. The area sits minutes from Eagle Creek Golf Club off Narcoossee Road, and the multi-acre lots common east of the corridor leave room for a full green with a chipping pad that a standard subdivision yard usually can't fit.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say you belong to Eagle Creek and want a green at home

Say a homeowner who plays Eagle Creek most weekends wants a 500 sq ft green with a two-cup layout and a small fringe apron, sited on the flat side yard of a two-acre Narcoossee lot. At the published $14–$30 per square foot range, that prices between about $7,000 and $15,000, with most builds like this landing near $9,000 to $12,500.

Because the lot's soil maps to Smyrna sand with a high seasonal water table, the crew builds the subbase four inches deep in two compacted lifts instead of one, and lasers the surface level before the carpet goes down. The result holds a truer, more predictable roll through a full rainy season than a shallower build would.

Room to build a real green, not a putting strip

A quarter-acre subdivision lot usually limits a green to a single contour and a couple of cups tucked against a fence line. A multi-acre Narcoossee property removes that ceiling: with side yard and open field to work with, a green can carry two or three pin positions, a proper fringe transition and a chipping pad set back far enough to actually swing into it, rather than the compressed layout a tight urban yard forces.

The tradeoff is that a bigger green needs a bigger, flatter subbase, and on ground with any natural roll to it, that means more grading before rock goes down than the green itself will ever show once it's finished.

Keeping light infill from sliding down a tiered green

A Narcoossee green's tiers create slopes a flat lawn never has to deal with, and infill brushed in at a light, even rate can still migrate slowly toward the lowest tier over months of rinsing and rain, thinning the higher ground while building up at the bottom. That's a version of the state's rule against infill leaving a property, just moving within the green's own footprint instead of off the lot entirely. A slightly heavier grooming pass on upper tiers during routine care, rather than a different infill product altogether, is usually enough to counter the drift before it changes how a ball rolls across the surface.

Golfers near Eagle Creek asking for a practice green at home

Eagle Creek Golf Club sits off Narcoossee Road, and its membership base is part of why putting greens come up more often here than in a non-golfing part of the county (Eagle Creek’s course details). A member who plays a course with fast, true greens usually wants the same speed at home, which is less about turf brand and more about how flat and firm the subbase compacts before the carpet ever goes down.

We ask about stimp speed preference and slope reading before ordering material, since a green built for casual chipping and one built to mimic tournament-speed greens use different pile heights and the same base method underneath either way.

Why a contoured green still needs an overall slope

Even with tiers and breaks built into the surface for play, a Narcoossee putting green's base still carries the same one to two percent overall grade toward a drainage point that any lawn does, so the two jobs, holding a shape and shedding water, happen at once rather than one after the other. A green shaped purely for interesting breaks without that underlying slope will hold water in its lowest tier after every storm, regardless of how well the ball rolls the rest of the time. Getting both requirements satisfied in the same base is what separates a green built by someone experienced with the shaping from a flat pad with decoration on top.

Setbacks for a green on a golf-community pond lot

A Narcoossee lot backing onto a pond or canal, common in golf-course communities, still has to keep a putting green at least ten feet from the water's edge unless a seawall separates the two, and the green can't be shaped to route drainage through a swale even where that would be the most convenient direction to send water. These setbacks sometimes conflict with where a homeowner pictures the green relative to the view, which is why confirming the buildable area against the property's actual waterline comes before any design work on breaks and tiers.

Infill and a roll test before calling the job done

The last step on a Narcoossee green is a thin, even layer of infill followed by a roll test, checking that a ball tracks true across the surface rather than pulling toward one side from uneven grooming or nap direction. Adjustments at this stage are usually small, a pass with the brush in a different direction, or a bit more infill in one section, rather than anything structural, since the base and surface work is already finished by this point. Skipping the roll test and assuming a green plays correctly because it looks finished is how a pulling break goes unnoticed until the first real game.

Brushing a green to keep the roll consistent

Consistency in a Narcoossee green's roll comes far more from regular grooming than from the age of the surface itself, which is why a light pass with a stiff brush, moving opposite the nap direction, belongs on a repeating schedule rather than a once-a-year task. Skipping several months between brushings lets the fiber settle into whatever direction foot traffic and rain have pushed it, and a ball crossing that section starts to pull slightly off line even though nothing about the green looks different to the eye. A gentle, frequent touch keeps the surface predictable in a way that one thorough grooming a year never quite manages.

Building a stable green on ground with a seasonal high water table

Narcoossee's flatwoods soil holds a water table that can sit within two to three feet of the surface for months, which is a problem for a putting green in a way it isn't for a plain lawn: a green that settles unevenly reads false, and a homeowner notices a bad roll long before they'd notice a lawn's minor dip. We compact the rock base in two full passes rather than one on any Narcoossee green, and check level with a laser rather than eyeballing it, since the margin for error on a green is a fraction of what it is on a residential lawn.

Questions people ask

Does a Narcoossee putting green need a permit separate from a lawn?

No. Osceola County reviews a putting green the same general way it reviews any other synthetic turf project, through ordinary landscape and drainage permitting rather than a golf-specific rule, since the county's code doesn't single out putting greens.

How much bigger can a green be on an acreage lot than in a typical subdivision?

There's no fixed limit, since price scales with square footage rather than lot size. What acreage actually buys is layout freedom: room for multiple cups, a real chipping approach and a fringe transition that a standard quarter-acre backyard usually has to compress or skip.

Do I need a well-water hookup to rinse a putting green?

A hose bib is all rinsing requires, and a private well feeds one exactly the way a Toho meter does. The green's irrigation heads, if any existed before, get capped the same as they would on a Toho-served lot.
